name: Punugulu
subtitle: crisp fermented-batter fritters, the roadside snack of the coast

ingredients.note: adds crispness, but it is wheat semolina — omit it to keep the punugulu gluten-free
only if the batter is young and not properly sour

prepNotes: Soak the rice and urad dal separately for 5 hours, then grind them together to a slightly coarse batter and leave it to ferment 8 to 10 hours somewhere warm.
The batter should be thicker than dosa batter and smell pleasantly sour — day-old dosa batter is exactly what most Andhra kitchens use.
Take the batter out of the fridge an hour before frying; cold batter drinks oil and stays heavy.

steps.text: Stir the rice flour and rava into the fermented batter and let it sit 15 minutes to hydrate.
steps.tip: This is what makes them crisp rather than bready. Do not skip the resting.

steps.text: Fold in the onion, green chillies, ginger, cumin, curry leaves, coriander leaves and salt.
steps.tip: Salt the batter just before frying — added early it thins the batter and the onion weeps.

steps.text: Check the consistency: it should drop off a spoon in a thick lump, not a ribbon. Add the baking soda only if the batter tastes flat.
Heat the oil in a kadhai to 170C — a drop of batter should sink briefly and rise within 3 seconds, fizzing.
steps.tip: Too hot and they brown outside while staying raw in the middle. This is the single most common failure.

steps.text: Drop in walnut-sized spoonfuls of batter, 8 or 10 at a time, keeping the pan uncrowded.
Fry 4 to 5 minutes, turning them once they float, until deep golden brown all over and audibly crisp when tapped with the spoon.
Lift them out onto a rack, not paper — paper traps steam and softens the bottoms.
Let the oil come back up to temperature for a minute before the next batch, and serve hot with coconut or peanut chutney.

storage: Eat within the hour — punugulu are a fresh-fried snack and go leathery once cool. The batter itself keeps 2 days refrigerated, so fry only what you will eat.
